title: Family pleaded for more mental-health care for man who killed 3 people
article: Abdulla Shaikh\'s killing spree, which left three random strangers dead, could have been prevented had Quebec\'s health system better handled his worsening mental health problems, one of his brothers told police.

His family couldn\'t understand why he was released from the hospital he was placed in after exhibiting bizarre behaviour in 2021, Sakir Shaikh told police this spring, in a statement that is part of the evidence at a coroner\'s inquest.
Abdulla had been hospitalized before. He had spent about a year in hospitals after being arrested in 2018 at Trudeau airport for being in a restricted area and burning his passport with a candle.
In August 2022, Abdulla, 26, shot and killed three people on Montreal and Laval streets within 24 hours before he was killed in an exchange of gunfire with police.
When Sakir was interviewed by police, an officer asked if the tragedy could have been prevented.
"Yes, if he had stayed in the hospital, because when he left the hospital, he stayed with my parents for a month" and then moved out and lived alone, Sakir said.
"My parents couldn\'t do anything. He had no followup except his appointments for his injections. We were all surprised when he left the hospital."
His brother\'s previous doctor had been "very strict and forced him to take his medication. He also consulted us."
The new doctor "was relaxed. Abdulla started being released (for brief periods) and a few months later (the doctor) let him out. He never consulted us," Sakir said.

Months before he was killed, an administrative tribunal decided Abdulla, who was diagnosed with schizophrenia, could continue residing outside a mental health institution. He had been released even though a psychiatrist determined he represented "a significant risk to public safety due to his mental state."
Coroner Géhane Kamel is conducting an inquiry into the deaths of Abdulla and his victims.
Testifying Wednesday, Sakir said his brother didn\'t show any signs of mental illness before 2018.
"Before that, he was very active, we worked out together, we played soccer and video games," Sakir said. "He wasn\'t a mean or threatening person."
Things changed in May 2018 when Abdulla started acting strangely.
In June, soon after he moved out of his parents\' house, he was stopped for the incident at Trudeau airport and charged with mischief, but was declared not criminally responsible.
When Sakir later asked Abdulla about that episode, his brother said he was hearing voices, and that he was cursed in Canada and had to leave the country.
Sakir said his brother was first held at the Philippe Pinel Institute, a psychiatric hospital, and later moved to the Cité-de-la-Santé Hospital in Laval, where he spent about a year.
Upon release, he said, Abdulla seemed better.
Within months he stopped taking his medication, saying he no longer needed it. Soon, his family saw symptoms they now know were related to his mental illness.

Around June 2020, Abdulla went missing for several days. He was tracked down in Pierrefonds. When Sakir arrived to meet him in an A&W parking lot, Abdulla told him he had run out of gas and had put water in the gas tank but the car wouldn\'t run. He hadn\'t slept or eaten in two days.
Sakir called Montreal police and two officers showed up.
"I told (one of the officers), \'I know my brother, he\'s not doing well, he\'s a danger to himself, he\'s a danger to others,\'" Sakir recalled at the inquest.
He said he urged the officers to take his brother to a hospital or to at least seize his car, but was told they couldn\'t because no crime was committed.
"I told them, \'Are we going to wait for him to commit a crime before we can stop him?\'"
Two weeks later, Sakir spoke to Abdulla\'s doctor\'s office and his brother was hospitalized again.
When he was let out in 2021, his family was taken aback.
"He wasn\'t like he used to be," Sakir said. "He didn\'t speak anymore."
Abdulla initially received monthly medical injections, but the schedule was changed to every three months. He was set to receive an injection a day or two after the day he was killed, Sakir said.
Kamel said the Shaikh family should not be ostracized.
"The choices or the decisions made by a member of our family don\'t belong to the rest of the family," she said.
She told Sakir she knows the family tried to help.
"It\'s not like you closed your eyes. You can only do what you can do. You can\'t follow him 24 hours a day."
The inquiry also heard Wednesday from an ex-girlfriend who, in 2016, filed a police report accusing Abdulla of sexual assault.

The woman, who is not being identified by the Montreal Gazette, told the inquiry Abdulla was physically and mentally abusive and that she was afraid of him during the last year of their three-year relationship.
She said he could become very aggressive in certain situations. Once, when she asked about bruises she noticed on him, he told her he got into a fight after being cut off while driving.
Abdulla always had money and she was under the impression that he was involved in fraud, she said.

He was involved in several alleged crimes dating back to 2015, of which none resulted in guilty verdicts. A summary of criminal cases includes allegations of threats, breaking and entering, credit card fraud and fleeing from police on a motorcycle.
